lessons.title: The electromagnetic spectrum and polarisation
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — electromagnetic waves, optics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the electromagnetic spectrum, its common properties and the uses and hazards of each region
Use c = fλ and calculate times of travel of signals
Explain polarisation as evidence that light is transverse and use Malus's law I = I₀cos²θ
reviewNotes: Approximate wavelength ranges for the bands are deliberately not given; the board may expect them.
Some syllabuses define microwaves/radio boundaries differently; 900 MHz for mobile networks is a typical figure (check local operators).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Electromagnetic waves
blocks.md:
Electromagnetic (e.m.) waves are oscillating, perpendicular electric and magnetic fields travelling together. They are **transverse**, need no medium, travel at **c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s** in vacuum, carry energy, and can be reflected, refracted, diffracted, polarised and can interfere.

In order of increasing frequency: **radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, γ-rays**. Always c = fλ.

blocks.title: Uses and hazards
blocks.md:
- Radio: broadcasting (FM, mobile networks). Microwaves: mobile phones, radar, satellite links, cooking.
- Infrared: remote controls, heaters, thermal imaging. Visible light: vision, optical fibres.
- UV: sterilising water, security marks; overexposure damages skin and eyes. X-rays: medical imaging; ionising. γ-rays: cancer treatment, sterilisation; highly ionising.

Higher-frequency radiation carries more energy per photon (E = hf), so is more hazardous.

items.text: all travel at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum

blocks.caption: The electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to γ-rays (not to scale).
blocks.alt: Seven coloured boxes in order: radio, microwaves, infrared, light, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma, with an arrow showing increasing frequency.

blocks.title: Polarisation
blocks.md:
In **plane-polarised** light the electric field oscillates in one plane only. Only transverse waves can be polarised, so polarisation shows light is transverse. A polaroid transmits only one plane: unpolarised light passing through one polaroid has its intensity **halved**.

For plane-polarised light incident on a second polaroid (analyser) at angle θ: **I = I₀ cos²θ** (Malus's law).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying sound can be polarised: sound is longitudinal.
- Forgetting the factor ½ when unpolarised light meets the first polaroid.
- Mixing up the order of the spectrum (gamma has the shortest wavelength).
- Using wavelengths in nm or cm without converting to metres.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Frequencies
blocks.statement: Find (a) the frequency of red light of wavelength 656 nm, (b) the wavelength of a 900 MHz mobile signal, (c) the time light takes to reach us from the Sun (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Two polaroids
blocks.statement: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a polaroid, then through a second polaroid whose axis is at 60° to the first. Find the final intensity.
steps: After the first polaroid: I₁ = I₀/2 (unpolarised light is halved).
After the second: I₂ = I₁ cos² 60° = (I₀/2) × (0.5)² = I₀/8.

lessons.title: Refraction, total internal reflection and lenses
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — electromagnetic waves, optics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use Snell's law n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ and the critical angle sin C = 1/n
Explain total internal reflection and the optical fibre
Use the thin-lens equation 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with the 'real is positive' convention and magnification m = v/u
reviewNotes: n for water 1.33 and glass 1.50 are typical values.
Real-is-positive sign convention is used; boards sometimes use Cartesian sign conventions — check.
Optical instruments (microscope, telescope) are not covered.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Refractive index
blocks.md:
The **refractive index** of a medium n = c/v (speed of light in vacuum ÷ speed in the medium). **Snell's law**: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, with angles measured from the **normal**. Light bends towards the normal on entering a denser medium (where it is slower and the wavelength is shorter; the frequency does not change).

Typical values: water 1.33, glass about 1.5.

blocks.title: Total internal reflection
blocks.md:
Light travelling from a denser medium to a less dense medium is totally reflected when the angle of incidence exceeds the **critical angle** C, where **sin C = 1/n** (for a boundary with air). Conditions: denser → less dense, and θ > C.

Uses: **optical fibres** (a core with a cladding of lower index), prisms in binoculars, reflectors. Fibres are used for telecommunications and endoscopes.

blocks.caption: A ray entering glass at 40° bends towards the normal (θ₂ = 25.4°).
blocks.alt: A ray in air hitting a glass block at 40 degrees from the dashed normal and bending to 25.4 degrees inside.

blocks.title: Thin lenses
blocks.md:
For a thin lens: **1/f = 1/u + 1/v** (real-is-positive convention: u and v positive for real objects/images; v negative for a virtual image; f positive for a converging lens, negative for a diverging one). Magnification **m = v/u** = image height ÷ object height. Power P = 1/f in dioptres (f in metres).

A converging lens gives a **real inverted** image if the object is beyond f and a **virtual magnified upright** image if it is within f (magnifying glass).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Measuring angles from the surface instead of from the normal.
- Trying to have total internal reflection going from air to glass: it only occurs from the denser to the less dense medium.
- Sign errors in the lens formula: a negative v means a virtual image on the same side as the object.
- Forgetting that frequency does not change on refraction (only speed and wavelength do).

blocks.title: Example 1 — Refraction in glass
blocks.statement: Light in air strikes glass (n = 1.50) at 40° to the normal. Find the angle of refraction and the speed of light in the glass.

blocks.title: Example 2 — A converging lens
blocks.statement: A converging lens has f = 10 cm. Find the image position and magnification for an object (a) 30 cm and (b) 5 cm from the lens.
steps: (b) 1/v = 1/10 − 1/5 = −1/10, so v = −10 cm (virtual, same side); m = −10/5 = −2 in this convention: magnified ×2 and upright.
blocks.answer: (a) v = 15 cm, m = 0.5; (b) v = −10 cm, magnified × 2

lessons.title: Diffraction gratings
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — electromagnetic waves, optics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State and use d sin θ = nλ for a diffraction grating and explain why the maxima are sharp
Determine wavelengths and the maximum number of orders, and describe the spectrum from white light
Compare the double-slit and the grating patterns and use the single-slit minimum a sin θ = λ
reviewNotes: The condition for the first minimum of a single slit is a sin θ = λ (small-angle form not used).
Normal incidence is assumed; oblique incidence is not covered.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The grating equation
blocks.md:
A **diffraction grating** has a large number of equally spaced parallel slits (often 300–600 lines per mm). Monochromatic light of wavelength λ gives bright maxima at angles θ given by **d sin θ = nλ**, where d is the slit spacing (d = 1/N for N lines per metre) and n = 0, 1, 2… is the **order**.

A large number of slits makes the maxima narrow and bright, so wavelengths can be measured accurately.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md:
1. Convert the line density to a spacing: d = 1/N (N in lines per metre; e.g. 300 lines/mm = 3.00 × 10⁵ m⁻¹, d = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m).
2. For a given order: sin θ = nλ/d.
3. The highest order occurs when sin θ ≤ 1: n_max is the largest integer ≤ d/λ.
4. The central maximum (n = 0) of white light is white; the higher orders are spectra with violet nearest the centre and red furthest.

blocks.caption: Diffraction by a grating: beams at angles θ given by d sin θ = nλ.
blocks.alt: A grating with a central beam and first and second order beams at angles above and below.

blocks.title: Single slit and comparisons
blocks.md:
A single slit of width a produces a wide central maximum with the first minimum at **a sin θ = λ**; a narrower slit gives a wider pattern. The double-slit fringes have an envelope given by the single-slit pattern.

The grating gives fewer, sharper and brighter maxima at larger angles than two slits of the same spacing.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the number of lines per mm directly as d: d is the reciprocal and must be in metres.
- Forgetting that n = 0 is a maximum (not counted among the 'orders' on each side).
- Counting the total number of maxima as 2n_max rather than 2n_max + 1.
- Saying red light is deviated less than violet: red has the longer wavelength, so it is deviated **more**.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Sodium light
blocks.statement: A grating has 300 lines per mm. Sodium light of wavelength 589 nm falls normally on it. Find the angles of the first and second orders and the maximum number of orders.
steps: d/λ = 5.66, so n_max = 5 (sin θ ≤ 1); the total number of maxima is 2 × 5 + 1 = 11.
blocks.answer: 10.2°, 20.7°; 5 orders each side; 11 maxima in all

blocks.title: Example 2 — Two wavelengths
blocks.statement: A grating with 500 lines per mm receives light containing 450 nm and 650 nm. Find the angular separation of the two first-order maxima.
